item.title: How My OPNsense Firewall Is Set Up
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: An overview of my network segmentation in OPNsense: six VLANs with different purposes, a base rule template that repeats across them (DNS, blocking private networks, default allow), VPN split tunneling through aliases and a dedicated gateway, and a look at the point-to-point rules for each segment.
item.content:encoded:
I already went deep on one specific piece of my firewall before - moving Traefik into its own VLAN, in «Traefik on Its Own VLAN - Setting Up the OPNsense Firewall». But that article only covered one segment (call it opt6) and the move of one specific service. In this one, I want to cover how my network segmentation works as a whole: how many VLANs I have, why each one exists, and the rule template that repeats almost unchanged across every segment.

How many VLANs, and why

flowchart LR
  WAN["WAN<br>internet"]
  LAN["LAN<br>main segment"]
  OPT1["opt1<br>WIFI"]
  OPT2["opt2<br>personal-use<br>hosts"]
  OPT3["opt3<br>DMZ for<br>YouTube filming"]
  OPT6["opt6<br>Traefik + CrowdSec"]

  WAN -->|"block GEOIP, block Firehol, block CrowdSec"| LAN
  LAN --- OPT1
  LAN --- OPT2
  LAN --- OPT3
  LAN --- OPT6

Six segments as of today.

The general principle behind the rules is the same across every segment, opt6 included - the base template below is identical everywhere. Within a segment, and from a segment out to the internet, access is pretty much unrestricted (it's a home network, not a corporate perimeter) - but between segments, access is closed by default. Every segment has a rule blocking access to other private networks sitting ahead of any allow rule (more on that below), and any cross-segment interaction gets its own specific rule. In opt6, that same point-to-point logic just scales up a lot harder than everywhere else - because that's where the reverse proxy and the security stack live (probably not even a full "stack," just CrowdSec, but who knows, maybe it'll grow into one), not workstations, and every proxied service gets its own dedicated exit point.

Because of that, the "Final rule" column in the table below isn't "what I allow by default" - it's the name of the last catch-all rule in each segment's chain. In other words, whatever's left allowed after the earlier blocking rules have already filtered out cross-segment traffic. The phrase "allow to any" in a rule's name can be misleading on its own - at the network level, the actual effect is the opposite: closed by default, and only what's explicitly described is open. I honestly couldn't find a cleaner way to show this without dumping every single rule into the table.

Segment Purpose Final rule
WAN External interface GeoIP, FireHOL, and CrowdSec blocks first, then 80 and 443 forwarded to Traefik - everything else inbound stays closed
LAN Main segment: workstations, NAS, admin access Default allow LAN to any (after blocking other segments)
opt1 WIFI Default allow WIFI to any (after blocking other segments)
opt2 Personal-use hosts Default allow to any (after blocking other segments)
opt3 DMZ Default allow DMZ to any (after blocking other segments)
opt6 Traefik + CrowdSec, its own perimeter (covered here) Default allow opt6 to any (after blocking, plus 50+ point-to-point allowances for proxied services)

WAN - what's open and what gets dropped at the door

The external interface is a lot simpler than the internal segments, but it's also where the first layer of filtering sits, so it gets its own section.

Exactly two ports are open to the outside world - 80 and 443. Both are forwarded through Destination NAT to a single LXC container running Traefik in opt6, and nowhere else. I don't keep any "just in case" forwards to individual services. Anything that's supposed to be reachable from the internet is reachable through Traefik and only through Traefik, and from there the point-to-point rules in opt6 take over (more on those below).

Traffic still has to make it to those two ports, though. The blocking rules on WAN sit above the allow rules, and they throw out a good chunk of the junk before it ever gets a look at Traefik.

flowchart LR
  I["Internet"] --> B["WAN<br>block GeoIP<br>block FireHOL<br>block CrowdSec"]
  B -->|"80, 443"| T["Traefik<br>LXC in opt6"]
  B -.->|"everything else"| X["dropped"]

There are three kinds of blocking here:

  • Country blocking (GeoIP) - a GeoIP alias backed by the MaxMind database. Inbound connections from countries I'm not expecting visitors from get dropped right away, before anything else is checked.
  • FireHOL blocklists - four of them at once, firehol_level1, firehol_level2, firehol_level3, and firehol_abusers_1d. These are addresses of botnets, scanners, command-and-control servers, and other hosts already caught doing something nasty. The lists are pulled by URL and refreshed by cron once a day.
  • CrowdSec right on OPNsense - the os-crowdsec plugin. Its Remediation Component blocks inbound connections at the firewall from any address CrowdSec has a ban decision for. Unlike the first two, this isn't a static list I wired in by hand - the set of addresses keeps changing on its own.

All three are set up exactly the way I walked through in «OPNsense 26.1 Install Guide - Firewall Setup From Scratch» - the aliases, excluding local networks from the FireHOL lists, block rules on WAN with direction in, a cron job for updates, and installing the CrowdSec plugin. In that guide I suggested most people start with firehol_level1 alone, while my own setup runs all four, the more aggressive ones included.

These filters don't duplicate each other. GeoIP is a blunt instrument that cuts off entire countries no matter how clean a given address is. FireHOL is targeted and catches addresses with a record, including ones from countries I haven't blocked. CrowdSec adds addresses banned for specific behavior on top of that - brute-forcing, scanning, that sort of thing.

Whatever gets past all of that and lands on 80 or 443 then runs into Traefik, which has another CrowdSec sitting next to it in opt6 (I've covered it separately, in Docker and in LXC). That one looks at the HTTP requests hitting specific services, which is exactly what the firewall can't see from where it sits.

One more detail that's easy to miss. The GeoIP and FireHOL rules live on WAN with direction in, so they only touch inbound connections. They have no effect on where my own devices go on the way out.

The base template that repeats in every segment

The same sequence of rules repeats almost identically across lan, opt1, opt2, opt3, and opt6:

  1. Allow internal DNS - lets the segment reach its own gateway IP on port 53. Without this rule, name resolution inside the segment just doesn't work, and everything else depends on resolving internal service hostnames.
  2. VPN split tunneling (see the dedicated section below) - routes specific categories of traffic through a VPN gateway instead of the default route.
  3. Block access to all other private networks - blocks this segment from reaching every other private range (the Private_Networks alias). This is the actual "closed by default" boundary between segments.
  4. Default allow <segment> to any (plus its IPv6 counterpart) - whatever hasn't been explicitly denied above, and isn't headed to another private segment, gets through. That's just how my home network is built: not zero-trust inside a segment, but tight control at the boundaries between segments.

lan also has:

  • Allow ICMP echo request messages - so plain ping works inside the network; this isn't on by default, it's a rule I added on purpose;
  • Allow admin devices access to anywhere without any restrictions (the admins alias) - a handful of devices (my own work machines) get explicit, unrestricted access everywhere, so I'm not fighting my own firewall while troubleshooting;
  • the same admin rule is duplicated in opt1.

You can build this template for your own VLANs in the OPNsense VLAN planner: enter your segments and the flows you allow, and it gives you the aliases and the rule order for every interface. The planner also blocks access to the firewall itself (This Firewall), so DNS is allowed with its own flow above that block - effectively the first step of the template.

VPN split tunneling - PROXYTUN

Every segment except the DMZ has a pair of policy-based routing rules with the same structure: traffic to a specific list of services (an alias along the lines of "I'm not telling, go figure it out yourself") gets rerouted through a separate gateway - PROXYTUN - instead of the normal route out to the internet.

The point of the whole setup: some services (broadly, foreign software resources, knowledge bases, and video hosting) aren't reachable just because, that's why (geo-blocking on their end, for instance - we're not breaking any Russian laws here), so that traffic needs to go out through the VPN, while everything else takes the normal route through the ISP. The service lists live in aliases, so adding or dropping a service is a one-alias edit, not a hunt through rules across all six segments.

Point-to-point cross-segment permissions

Beyond the base template, every segment has its own set of point-to-point rules for specific services - but how many there are, and what they cover, varies a lot:

  • opt1 (WIFI) - literally a handful of specific allowances for individual devices to individual services (the media server, Traefik, and so on), nothing more.
  • opt2 (personal-use hosts) - the busiest of the "regular" segments by rule count: access to a database (an external Postgres instance, in my case) from several sources, access to a couple of internal services, and access to the NAS over file-sharing protocols (specific ports, in other words). Most of the exceptions end up here, because this segment has the most varied mix of services.
  • opt3 (DMZ) - the bare minimum: essentially just the base template, no point-to-point rules at all. Makes sense for a DMZ - that's where everything you see me film for the channel lives, so getting in from the outside world isn't happening. And even if it somehow did, congrats, you get to sit alone in that VLAN.
  • opt6 (Traefik/CrowdSec) - built on a fundamentally different model than the rest, so I'll cover it separately below.
  • lan - doesn't stop at the base template either. A handful of rules shaped like "host → Traefik:443" exist for specific services in the main segment that need access to proxied resources. Same logic as the "from other segments to Traefik" direction covered below - just at the level of individual hosts instead of the whole segment.

opt6 - point-to-point access on top of the base template

The base template is right here too, default allow included, same as everywhere else - but on top of it, instead of one blanket "Traefik can see the whole homelab" rule, there are 50+ individual point-to-point rules, one per proxied service:

flowchart LR
  T["Traefik<br>opt6"] -->|":service A port"| A["Service A"]
  T -->|":service B port"| B["Service B"]
  T -->|":service C port"| C["Service C"]
  T -.->|"~50 other services"| D["..."]

Back when Traefik was physically a friendly neighbor neighboring container on the same host and the same Docker box as most of the services, this level of detail wasn't needed - traffic never even left the Docker bridge network. Once Traefik moved to its own VLAN, every single interaction started crossing a segment boundary, and the firewall finally saw (and could restrict) something that used to be completely invisible to it.

Just as important - and easy to overlook - is access the other way, from the rest of the segments to Traefik:443:

flowchart LR
  subgraph Others["LAN / opt1 / opt2"]
    S["Services and agents"]
  end
  S -->|"regular reverse-proxy traffic"| T["Traefik:443<br>opt6"]
  S -->|"ForwardAuth / OIDC"| T
  S -->|"WSS agents (e.g. Periphery)"| T

Technically, this isn't one rule for the whole segment but a set of point-to-point rules of the form "specific host → Traefik:443": access to Traefik is opened only for whoever actually needs it. The DMZ is deliberately left out of that list - nothing there talks to Traefik.

Without these rules, three things break at once: external routing, ForwardAuth/OIDC authentication, and the WSS connections used by background agents - because all three scenarios technically travel the exact same path over port 443, not three separate ones. This isn't a patch for a specific problem, it's a direct consequence of Traefik being a single entry point for people, services, and agents all at once. So whenever I set up a new segment, I have to put this path in from the start, or nothing will work. Of course, I do forget about it every now and then - but a service that suddenly stops working is always happy to remind me.

A detailed walkthrough of the move into this segment (what it looked like before, what changed, what the audit turned up) is in a separate article.

What's next

  • A more detailed look at opt1 (WIFI) and opt3 (DMZ) as their own articles, if I end up with enough interesting material. Right now there just isn't enough going on there to be worth a write-up.
  • If I ever spin up another segment for something new, I'll follow the same template: DNS, VPN split tunneling if needed, blocking private networks, a default allow, and point-to-point rules on top of that.

Links

  • Traefik on Its Own VLAN - Setting Up the OPNsense Firewall - a detailed breakdown of the opt6 segment
  • OPNsense 26.1 Install Guide - Firewall Setup From Scratch - step-by-step setup of GeoIP blocking, FireHOL lists, and the CrowdSec plugin
  • OPNsense VLAN Planner - aliases and rule order for your own segments

item.title: OPNsense 26.1 Install Guide - Firewall Setup From Scratch
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: A practical guide to OPNsense 26.1 - installing on bare metal, configuring the firewall, GeoIP, FireHOL and CrowdSec, plus network monitoring and protecting your home lab.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Let's dig into setting up OPNsense 26.1, that gateway/firewall you've probably already heard of.

Note

This is, as far as I know, the only guide of its kind in Russian - it took a genuinely absurd amount of time and effort to put together. If it helps you out and you feel like buying the author a coffee, there's a Boosty link for that.

My site already has a fair amount of OPNsense content scattered around, but for anyone just starting out it's all over the place and hard to stitch together into a coherent picture. So, mustering whatever willpower I had left, I finally sat down to write this thing - my own little Sisyphean task.

What OPNsense Actually Is

OPNsense is a free, open-source firewall/router distro built on top of FreeBSD. It turns a regular PC, a mini-PC, or even a VM into a full-blown, enterprise-grade network appliance.

People tend to call it "just a firewall," but that undersells it quite a bit. On top of filtering traffic, it can moonlight as a router, VPN gateway, DHCP/DNS server, load balancer, reverse proxy, IDS/IPS - basically a one-stop shop for network security.

Note

A few features, like the reverse proxy, need a plugin installed first.

One of the best things about OPNsense is that it packs all this functionality behind a genuinely usable web UI, with regular updates on top. You can get almost everything done through the GUI - no need to live in a terminal.

How OPNsense Stacks Up Against the Alternatives

The usual suspects you'll be comparing it to are pfSense, MikroTik RouterOS, OpenWrt, and the classic "hand-rolled Linux box acting as a router."

What sets OPNsense apart is its focus on ease of administration, a transparent development process, and a steady stream of updates. It started life as a pfSense fork (which is itself a fork), and from day one it leaned hard into open development, a modern management UI, and a release cycle you can actually plan around.

Against MikroTik RouterOS, OPNsense wins on security features and how easily you can bolt on extra services - and no offense to the Mikrotik crowd, but OPNsense is just plain easier to configure. OpenWrt, meanwhile, is really built for home routers and is honestly closer to "an OS for aging router hardware" than a serious platform - OPNsense, by contrast, happily runs on dedicated network appliances just as well as on ordinary x86 boxes and VMs.

And compared to rolling your own router on Linux, OPNsense saves you from having to bolt together a firewall, DHCP, DNS, VPN, and monitoring by hand. It's all baked into one platform, accessible from a single web interface.

What You'd Actually Use It For

OPNsense fits just as well in a home network as it does in small-to-medium business infrastructure. The usual use cases:

  • sharing one internet connection across multiple networks and VLANs;

  • setting firewall rules and segmenting the network;

  • running VPN servers and clients (WireGuard, OpenVPN, IPsec);

  • handling DHCP and DNS;

  • publishing internal services through a reverse proxy;

  • locking things down with IDS/IPS, GeoIP filtering, and other security tools;

  • keeping an eye on network activity and digging through event logs;

  • setting up high availability (HA) and redundant network infrastructure.

OPNsense on a Home Lab

If you're running a homelab, OPNsense can easily become the centerpiece of your network - it lets you build something that looks and behaves a lot like a corporate setup, minus the expensive gear and the CCNA.

Typical homelab use: separate VLANs for servers, workstations, IoT junk, and guests; secure remote access over VPN; publishing services to the internet (there's a Caddy reverse-proxy plugin for that); firewalling between segments; and having one place to manage network security instead of five.

Since it virtualizes well, OPNsense runs great in Proxmox VE and other hypervisors - so you don't necessarily need a dedicated box for it. That said, for max performance and reliability, a lot of people still like to put it on a small dedicated mini-PC with a couple of NICs.

Note

In the video linked above, I set everything up on a mini-PC with two physical NICs, so that's the configuration this article follows for installation and initial setup. Everything past that point applies regardless of whether you're running virtualized or on bare metal.

Installing OPNsense

Picking an Installation Image

First, grab the installer image from the project's official site. There are a bunch of options listed, but picking the right one boils down to one question: where is this going to run?

Installing on a physical box or mini-PC with a monitor and keyboard hooked up? Grab the VGA image - that's what I use in this article.

The DVD image is aimed at virtual machines and works fine for Proxmox VE, VMware, Hyper-V, and friends.

Got a serial console, managing things over a COM port? That's the Serial image - more common on industrial gear and certain networking appliances.

There's also a Nano image on the downloads page, but you'll almost never need it - the devs point everyone toward a normal install with VGA, DVD, or Serial.

Making a Bootable USB Drive

Once you've downloaded it, flash the image onto a USB stick with Rufus, balenaEtcher, or whatever else you like for writing bootable images.

When it's done, plug the drive into the machine you're installing on and pick it as the boot device from BIOS/UEFI.

Running Through the Installer

I'm skipping screenshots here to keep the article from ballooning any further.

  • Don't press any key when the Configuration Importer prompt appears.
  • When prompted for Manual Interface Assignment, press any key. I prefer to configure interfaces manually rather than use automatic configuration.
  • Press Enter to skip LAGG configuration.
  • Press Enter to skip VLAN creation (we'll configure them later through the web interface).
  • Enter igc0 as the WAN interface name.
  • Enter igc1 as the LAN interface name.
  • When prompted for an Optional Interface Name, press Enter to skip this step (we'll configure additional interfaces later).
  • Press Y, then Enter to continue.
  • At the login prompt, enter the username installer and password opnsense to begin the installation.
  • Press Enter to use the default keyboard layout (if you're using a US keyboard; otherwise select the appropriate option).

Next up, the installer asks you to pick a file system - ZFS or UFS.

UFS is the classic FreeBSD file system. It's lighter on resources and does the job for most home routers, but it's more "brittle" than ZFS.

ZFS brings extras like data-integrity checking, snapshots, and much more flexible storage management - at the cost of wanting more RAM and CPU.

For a homelab and most modern mini-PCs, I'd go with ZFS, especially if you're installing to an SSD and have at least 8 GB of RAM to spare. If you're running OPNsense as a virtual router though, keep in mind that stacking ZFS on top of ZFS isn't exactly a great idea - either way, the right filesystem really depends on your specific setup.

Warning

Skip the cheap no-name SSDs and NVMe drives here, especially if you're pairing them with ZFS. OPNsense writes a ton of logs as a firewall, and ZFS writes plenty of its own on top - budget drives under that kind of sustained write load tend to die fast.

Once you've picked a filesystem, you'll select the drive to install onto. Double- and triple-check you've picked the right disk before confirming - everything on it gets wiped.

When the file copy wraps up, the installer will ask you to set a root password. Do it right then and there, so you're not still running the default password after your first boot.

Initial Setup

Once OPNsense reboots after the install, it drops you into a console menu right on the attached monitor - that's also where you'll see whatever IP address it handed the LAN interface (by default that's 192.168.1.1/24, and OPNsense starts acting as a DHCP server for LAN the moment the install finishes). Everything from here on happens in the web UI - we're done with the console.

Logging into the web UI for the first time

Plug your laptop into the LAN port (directly, or through a switch) - it should grab an address over DHCP automatically - then open https://192.168.1.1 in a browser (or whatever address the console showed you).

Your browser is going to throw a certificate warning right away - that's expected, it's a self-signed cert. I walked through swapping it for a real Let's Encrypt cert in my Proxmox ACME article - OPNsense has its own built-in ACME client too, and the concept is identical, but that's a separate rabbit hole. For now, just click through the warning.

Log in as root with the password you set at the very end of the installer.

Running through the Setup Wizard

The first time you log in, OPNsense offers to walk you through its Setup Wizard. It's entirely optional - you can close it and configure everything by hand through the individual menus instead - but on a brand-new box it's the fastest way to get the basics out of the way. Here's what each screen does:

  1. General Information - set the Hostname (say, opnsense) and Domain (your real domain, or a placeholder like home.arpa if you don't have one handy). Together they form the box's full name (opnsense.stilicho.ru), which later shows up in certificates, DHCP leases, and logs.
  2. Time Server Information - your time zone and an NTP server. The default NTP pool is fine unless you have a reason to point at something else - accurate time matters a lot here, for certs, logs, and IDS/IPS working correctly.
  3. Configure WAN Interface - this re-asks the same WAN questions (DHCP/Static/PPPoE) you already answered in the console installer. If WAN's already up and working, just click through this screen without touching anything. Worth noting: two checkboxes further down, Block private networks and Block bogon networks - leave both enabled on your internet-facing interface. They drop packets carrying private or unallocated ("bogon") source addresses, which have no business showing up on WAN in the first place, and that alone quietly cuts a good chunk of noise out of your firewall logs.
  4. Configure LAN Interface - the IP and subnet for LAN. The default (192.168.1.1/24) is fine to keep, or change it now to whatever you'd rather use - just know that changing it will drop your current browser session, and you'll need to reconnect at the new address.
  5. Set the root password - reset it here if you want, or just skip past it.
  6. Reloading package configuration - the wizard applies everything you entered; if you changed the LAN subnet in step 4, the address in your browser's URL bar is about to change out from under you.
Note

You can re-run the wizard any time from System → Wizard - handy if you want to start over from scratch after a factory reset.

Checking for updates

Right after the wizard, it's worth checking whether anything's shipped since the install image was built. Head to System → Firmware → Status and hit Check for updates. If there's anything newer, switch to the Updates tab and click Update (a major version jump, say from 25.x to 26.x, will ask you to confirm and may reboot once or twice on its own).

Tip

While you're in there, take a look at System → Firmware → Plugins too - the official plugin list includes os-crowdsec and the Caddy reverse-proxy plugin, both of which come up later in this article. You don't need to install either one right now, but it's good to know they're sitting right there instead of hunting for them online as if they were third-party add-ons.

General settings (System → Settings → General)

A few fields here are worth double-checking even if you already ran the wizard:

  • Hostname / Domain - same values you set in the wizard; you can rename the box here later if you change your mind.
  • DNS servers - fine to leave blank or at the defaults for now. Once you get to the Unbound DNS section below, leaving this field empty becomes a deliberate choice rather than an oversight - I explain why right there.
  • DNS server options - uncheck Allow DNS server list to be overridden by DHCP/PPP on WAN if you're planning to run your own resolver (Unbound or Dnsmasq) - otherwise your ISP's DNS servers can quietly sneak back into the config on top of yours.
  • Language and Top navigation - purely cosmetic. I leave the UI in English, since every doc page and forum post I need to cross-reference is in English too, and it's a lot less friction matching what's on screen to what you're reading online.

Web UI and SSH access

Over in System → Settings → Administration, a few settings are worth locking down early:

  • TCP port - the web UI's port, 443 by default. If you're planning to also run OPNsense as a reverse proxy on port 443 for internal services down the line, it'll collide with the admin UI on that same port - move the admin port to something non-standard now (8443, say) and save yourself the headache later.
  • Listen Interfaces - leave it blank and the web UI listens on every interface, WAN included. You almost never need admin access from outside your own network - restrict this explicitly to LAN (and a management VLAN, if you're running one), so the web UI simply isn't reachable from the internet, regardless of what your firewall rules say.
  • Secure Shell, further down the same page - turns on SSH access to the OPNsense shell. It's off by default; only flip it on if you actually need it (troubleshooting CrowdSec later in this article is a good example), and when you do, move it off port 22 and lock it down to specific source IPs with a firewall rule.

That's the box squared away - from here we'll get into DNS, VLANs, firewall rules, and locking the whole thing down against attacks.

Setting Up Unbound DNS

Unbound is a validating, recursive, caching DNS resolver built for speed and security. It's open-source, BSD-licensed, built by NLnet Labs, and it's the thing quietly resolving domain names to IP addresses behind the scenes on a huge number of platforms. Sysadmins, ISPs, and privacy nerds all lean on it heavily, and it plays nicely with OPNsense, pfSense, FreeBSD, Linux, macOS, and pretty much any other Unix-like OS.

I'm only going to cover the core Unbound features here, as they apply inside OPNsense.

What Unbound Brings to the Table

Unbound supports DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions), which vouches for the authenticity and integrity of DNS data and protects you from things like DNS spoofing or cache poisoning. It can also do recursive queries and cache the results, which speeds up repeat lookups noticeably.

A quick rundown of what Unbound gives you:

  • Efficiency and lightness: designed to use minimal resources.
  • Configuration flexibility: supports a wide range of configuration options for complex, advanced setups.
  • DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS: encrypts DNS queries to improve privacy.
  • IPv6 support: fully compatible with modern internet protocols.
  • Access control: lets you configure which clients are allowed to make DNS queries to the server.

Unfortunately, Unbound's settings page is deep enough that covering every option properly would take several articles on its own, so I'll just drop screenshots of how I set it up in the video instead.

Here's the General section:

And the Advanced section:

Setting Up DNS over TLS

DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypts your DNS queries so they can't be casually snooped on or tampered with in transit. OPNsense lets you turn this on using the built-in Unbound resolver.

What follows is the short version - for the full walkthrough with all the details, see my dedicated articles on DNS over TLS in OPNsense and its alternative, DNS over HTTPS in OPNsense via DNSCrypt-proxy.

How It Works

By default, DNS queries fly across the network completely in the clear. Your ISP - or anyone else in the middle - can watch UDP/TCP traffic on port 53 and see exactly what domains you're resolving, or worse, mess with the answers. That's the whole reason to encrypt DNS in the first place. DNS over TLS (DoT) uses TLS to wrap your DNS traffic and is one of the more widely adopted ways to do this. The point is simple: more privacy, more security. A few concrete benefits:

  • Attackers can't quietly tamper with your DNS responses.
  • It kills man-in-the-middle attacks - the kind where your request gets hijacked and redirected to a phishing page.
  • It's supposed to stop eavesdropping too, though let's be honest, for a home network that benefit is mostly theoretical.

Turning On DoT in OPNsense

Here's how to get DoT configured and running on your OPNsense box:

  1. Go to "Services" → "Unbound DNS" → "DNS over TLS" in the OPNsense web interface.

  1. Click the "+" Add button in the bottom-right corner of the panel.
  2. Make sure the "Enabled" option is checked.
  3. You can leave the Domain field empty - that way every query gets sent to the server you specify below. Fill in a domain name instead, and only queries for that specific domain get routed to this server.
  4. Enter the IP address of the DNS server to forward all queries to, for example 8.8.8.8.
  5. Set the server port for DoT to 853.
  6. Enter the DNS server's common name (for example, dns.google.com) in the Verify CN field so its TLS certificate can be validated. Without certificate verification, DoT is wide open to man-in-the-middle attacks. You can leave this blank to accept self-signed certs, but doing so basically defeats the whole point of this exercise.

  1. Click "Save".
  2. You can add an IPv6 DNS server as a secondary resolver.
  3. Click "Apply" to activate the settings.

In the end you'll get something like this.

Making DNS and DHCP Play Along

Just enabling DoT isn't enough - you need to force every client on the network to actually use those DoT servers, which means touching your DNS and DHCP settings too:

  1. Go to System → Settings → General in the left-hand menu.
  2. Make sure every DNS server field is empty. That keeps DNS traffic routed back through the router itself.

Setting Up the DHCP Server

ISC (Internet Systems Consortium) built and maintained the open-source ISC DHCP server for years - but active development on it stopped back in October 2022.

Its official successor is Kea DHCP, also from ISC.

Through OPNsense 25.7, ISC DHCP was the default. Starting with 25.7, that job passed to Dnsmasq DNS and DHCP instead, since it's lightweight and a good fit for small networks. OPNsense still ships Kea DHCP too, so you're free to pick whichever suits your setup better.

I've got a separate article on migrating from ISC to KEA, but here I'll just walk through the Dnsmasq side of things.

Note

Some parts of the video (and this article) are optional - not everyone needs static DHCP reservations or domain/host overrides.

Dnsmasq or Kea?

The choice here comes down less to raw performance and more to what you're actually trying to do.

Dnsmasq DHCP

For most home users and small homelabs, Dnsmasq is the way to go - which is exactly why it's the default now.

Dnsmasq fits well if:

  • your home network or homelab consists of several VLANs and doesn't need complex DHCP infrastructure;

  • you want to use Dnsmasq not just as a DHCP server, but also as a DNS forwarder instead of Unbound DNS;

  • you need device names obtained via DHCP to automatically register in the local DNS server;

  • you plan to use OPNsense's special DNS aliases to block access to certain domains.

Kea DHCP

Kea DHCP is ISC DHCP's modern successor, aimed at meatier use cases.

Reach for it if:

  • you need DHCP high availability;

  • your network has fancier routers that need IPv6 prefix delegation.

And What About DNS?

Beyond DHCP, you've also got a DNS service to pick. OPNsense gives you two: Dnsmasq DNS and Unbound DNS.

Even though Dnsmasq took over as the default DHCP server, Unbound is still the primary DNS server here. Each has its own strengths.

Dnsmasq DNS

Dnsmasq makes sense when:

  • you want to use DHCP and DNS within a single service;

  • you need support for OPNsense DNS aliases, which automatically resolve domain names to IP addresses for use in firewall rules;

  • you need the simplest possible DNS configuration without a lot of extra settings.

That said, Dnsmasq is noticeably less capable than Unbound overall - fewer configuration knobs, and much thinner logging/diagnostics for DNS queries.

Unbound DNS

Unbound is OPNsense's default DNS server, and the one I'd recommend to most people.

What it brings to the table:

  • it's a full recursive DNS resolver that can query the root DNS servers directly, without relying on public DNS providers;

  • it supports DNS Block Lists (DNSBL), letting you block ads, trackers, and malicious domains, similar to Pi-hole;

  • it supports DNS over TLS (DoT), so DNS queries can be sent encrypted through trusted DNS servers such as Cloudflare or Quad9;

  • it provides detailed statistics and reports on DNS activity in the Reporting section, which significantly simplifies diagnostics and query analysis.

One gotcha: once you turn on DNS over TLS, Unbound stops acting as a recursive resolver and instead just forwards everything to whatever external server you picked, over an encrypted connection.

Running Dnsmasq and Unbound Side by Side

Sometimes it's worth running both at once.

For instance: Dnsmasq handles DHCP while Unbound stays the primary DNS server. Clients keep sending their DNS queries to Unbound as usual, and anything asking for a local hostname gets automatically forwarded over to Dnsmasq, which already knows about every device that grabbed an address via DHCP.

That gets you the best of both worlds - Unbound's more advanced feature set, plus automatic name resolution for everything on the local network.

Setting Up the Firewall

Time to cover the basics of packet filtering in OPNsense - how firewall rules get built and applied, with a few simple examples along the way.

How the OPNsense Firewall Actually Works

Here are the core concepts you need before any of the packet filtering stuff makes sense.

Rules

OPNsense runs on a Stateful Packet Filter - it decides what traffic is allowed to move between networks, and how packets get forwarded through the box.

Firewall rules here are just security policies attached to traffic, organized per interface.

The building blocks of a rule, below.

Actions

Every rule gets one of three actions.

Pass (Allow)

Lets the traffic through.

Block

Drops the traffic silently - the client gets no indication anything happened.

This is what you want for untrusted networks, i.e. the internet.

Reject

Drops the traffic and tells the client about it.

Only works for TCP and UDP:

  • TCP gets an RST (Reset) packet;
  • UDP gets an ICMP Destination Unreachable back.
Note

Note On internal networks, Reject is usually the friendlier choice - the client finds out immediately instead of sitting around waiting for a timeout. On untrusted networks like the internet, go with Block instead - no point handing a would-be attacker any extra information about how your firewall behaves.

The "Allow All" Rule

Once you've finished the initial LAN/WAN setup, OPNsense quietly drops in a few default rules for you:

  • an anti-lockout rule (Web Administration Anti-Lockout Rule);
  • an Allow All rule for IPv4;
  • an Allow All rule for IPv6.

Two things these rules do for you:

  • keep you from accidentally locking yourself out of the OPNsense web UI;
  • give LAN devices full access to the internet and anything else behind the firewall.

So anything plugged straight into the router - or into a switch hanging off it - gets online immediately, no extra rule-writing required.

Delete or disable Allow All, though, and all outbound LAN traffic gets blocked. The one thing that keeps working is access to OPNsense's own web UI.

Why You'd Turn Off Anti-Lockout on a Corporate Network

Anti-Lockout is great for home use, but it's a liability in a corporate setting.

The problem: it lets any device on the LAN reach the firewall's management interfaces, including:

  • the Web GUI;
  • the SSH console.

Not exactly a comforting thought from a security standpoint - that's a straight line to compromise or data leaks.

So on a corporate network, you'd want to:

  1. turn off Anti-Lockout;
  2. write your own rule that only lets admins or trusted devices in.

Looking at the Default Rules

Want to see what OPNsense created automatically?

  1. Go to Firewall → Rules → LAN.
  2. At the top of the rule list, click the dropdown icon next to Automatically generated rules.

That'll show you the automatically created rules, including:

  • Default Anti-Lockout Rule;
  • Allow LAN to Any.

The Order OPNsense Checks Rules In

When a packet shows up, OPNsense walks through rules in this order:

  1. Floating Rules;
  2. Interface Groups (group-level rules);
  3. Interface Rules (rules on individual interfaces).

The auto-generated system rules typically land at the front of that queue.

Quick, and How It Changes Rule Matching

Most rules ship with Quick turned on by default.

With Quick enabled, it's simple:

Note

First Match Wins.

The moment a packet matches a rule:

  • checking stops right there;
  • everything after it gets ignored.

Turn Quick off, and the logic flips:

Note

Last Match Wins.

You'll rarely need this mode - it's really only for specialized filtering policies.

The standard Default Deny rule is a good example of exactly this mechanism: no matching rule means the packet gets dropped.

Why Order Matters So Much

Rules get evaluated top to bottom, full stop.

Which means where you put a rule directly decides what happens to matching traffic.

The instant a packet hits a rule -

  • Pass;
  • Block;
  • Reject,

processing stops right there.

That's the whole reason behind the standard advice:

  • specific rules go near the top;
  • broad, catch-all ones go near the bottom.

A typical layout:

  1. let LAN users through on HTTP and HTTPS only;
  2. then allow DNS;
  3. add whatever else you actually need;
  4. finish with a Deny All or Allow All rule to mop up anything left over.

Do it this way and the config stays readable, and your security posture is noticeably better for it.

Traffic Direction

Rules apply in one of two directions:

  • Incoming (In);
  • Outgoing (Out).

OPNsense defaults to filtering incoming traffic (In).

Which means: build the rule on whichever interface the packet arrives on.

For Example

Say you want to let HTTPS (port 443) traffic from the internet reach an internal web server. The rule goes on the WAN interface, since that's where packets from the outside world first hit OPNsense. From there it'll allow incoming TCP 443 connections to your server.

Aliases are one of the best tools OPNsense gives you - they cut down your rule count massively and keep the whole configuration readable.

An alias is basically a named list of:

Leaning on the built-in ones alone makes your rules a lot easier to read at a glance.

Why Bother With Aliases

They let you:

  • write clearer rules;

  • make the configuration easier to maintain;

  • reduce the number of rules;

  • combine many objects into a single rule;

  • improve firewall performance by reducing the number of rules that need to be checked.

Basically, well-organized aliases can take a genuinely nasty configuration and make it manageable.

1. Locking Clients to Specific DNS Servers

One of the first security wins worth grabbing is blocking third-party DNS. That stops users - or malware - from routing around your filtering policies, parental controls, or DNS-based blocklists.

The idea is to only let clients talk to:

  • OPNsense's own built-in DNS server;

  • your own local DNS server;

  • or a trusted external DNS service that does filtering.

You'll need two rules for this.

OPNsense always has an implicit Deny All at the very end of its rule list.

So admins typically flip that around and explicitly allow only what's actually needed.

Home users, though, often struggle to enumerate every port a modern gadget wants to talk on:

  • TVs;

  • game consoles;

  • smartphones;

  • laptops;

  • IoT devices.

Which is why home networks often end up structured like this instead:

  1. block rules at the top;

  2. followed by whatever allow rules you actually need;

  3. an Allow All rule tacked on at the very end.

Makes running a home network a lot less painful - though I wouldn't recommend this pattern for corporate infrastructure.

5. Giving the Admin Unrestricted Access

When you're troubleshooting, you often just need to reach any device on the network, fast.

Worth having a dedicated rule for this that sits above every block rule.

5.1 The Alias

Create:

and drop into it:

  • the admin's work computer;

  • their laptop;

  • an administration server;

  • anything else trusted.

5.2 The Rule
Parameter Value
Action Pass
Interface LAN
Protocol any
Source admins
Destination any
Destination Port any
Description Allow admin devices access to anywhere without any restriction

On whichever interface the admin's devices live (usually LAN):

  1. create a Pass rule;

  2. set the source to admins;

  3. leave everything else at Any.

This gets administrators into any device on the network, ignoring whatever other restrictions are in place.

Since OPNsense processes top-down, put this one right at the top of the list.

Destination NAT (Port Forward)

What Port Forwarding Actually Does

When several devices on a local network hide behind a single external IP, every incoming connection from the internet lands on that same address.

Without extra config, OPNsense has no idea which internal device an incoming connection is actually meant for - so it just gets rejected.

Destination NAT (DNAT), better known as Port Forward, is the fix.

The classic case: publishing an internal web server. To make it reachable, forward incoming connections on:

  • 80/TCP (HTTP);
  • 443/TCP (HTTPS).

Where to Configure This

Head to:

Firewall → NAT → Destination NAT (Port Forward)

You'll see every existing DNAT rule here, plus the usual create/edit/delete controls.

The Core DNAT Fields

Here's what you'll be filling in when creating a new rule.

Parameter Description
Disabled Disables the rule without deleting it. While this option is enabled, the rule doesn't apply.
Sequence Sets where the rule falls in the processing order - OPNsense works through rules top to bottom.
Categories Lets you assign the rule one or more categories for easier organization and filtering.
Description A free-text description of the rule. Give it a clear name so you can tell what it's for at a glance later.

Interface Fields

You'll also need to say which interface and traffic type the rule targets.

Parameter Description
Interface Which interface (or interfaces) receive the incoming traffic. Usually WAN, since that's what you're publishing services on.
Version The IP protocol version the rule applies to: IPv4, IPv6, or both at once.
Protocol The protocol the rule has to match. Most of the time that's TCP, UDP, or a TCP/UDP combo, but other protocols are supported too.

Getting the Source Fields Right

Filtering and NAT rules both hinge on defining the source correctly.

Parameter Description
Invert Source Flips the source match: instead of matching the specified range, the rule matches everything except it. For example, "everything except 192.168.1.0/24".
Source Address Specifies the source network, IP address, or alias the traffic should come from. You can use individual hosts, entire networks, or groups.
Source Port Defines the source port or port range. Rarely used, since client ports are usually assigned dynamically - but it can come in handy for specialized filtering.

And the Destination Fields

Just as important - nailing down exactly where the traffic is going. That's what the Destination fields handle.

Parameter Description
Invert Destination Flips the destination match: instead of the specified address or network, the rule applies to everything except it.
Destination Address The IP address, network, or alias traffic should be directed to. Can include individual hosts or address groups.
Destination Port The destination port or port range. Used to filter specific services (for example, HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, etc.).

Redirect / Translation Fields

These decide exactly where incoming traffic actually ends up once the rule fires.

💡 How It Works

NAT translation swaps the original external destination (say, your firewall's public IP) for the internal server's address.

For example:

  • external IP: 203.0.113.10:443

  • internal server: 192.168.1.50:443

Once the rule's live, the connection gets redirected to the internal host automatically.

Redirection Fields

Parameter Description
Redirect Target IP The internal IP address incoming traffic will be redirected to. Usually a server on the local network (LAN or DMZ).
Redirect Target Port The port on the internal host that the connection will be redirected to. It can match the external port or differ from it (for example, 80 → 8080).
Pool Options Controls how traffic gets spread across multiple internal IPs - load balancing, or picking a target via a specific algorithm.

A Few More DNAT Options

There are also some extra knobs governing how the rule behaves, syncs, and interacts with the rest of your firewall rules.

Options Fields
Parameter Description
No XMLRPC Sync Excludes this rule from synchronization with HA (High Availability) partners. Used in clusters where not all NAT rules should be copied to the secondary node.
NAT Reflection Controls NAT reflection (hairpin NAT) mode. Lets internal clients reach services via the external IP address. Can be enabled, disabled, or inherit the global setting.
Set Tag Assigns a tag to packets matching this NAT rule. Used for further processing by other firewall rules.
Match Tag Lets the rule apply only to packets that already carry a specific tag. Used for complex routing and filtering scenarios.

Firewall Rule (Auto-Generating Rules from NAT)

OPNsense can spin up matching firewall rules automatically based on your NAT config.

Your options:

Option Description
Manual (recommended) The administrator manually creates the firewall rules. This is the most flexible and recommended option.
Pass (auto rule) Automatically allows traffic matching the NAT rule. These rules don't appear on the Firewall Rules tab.
Generate Interface Rules Automatically creates rules on the interface, which can then be overridden by higher-priority rules.

A Word of Caution

A few things worth keeping in mind if you go with auto-generated rules:

  • the NAT rule and firewall rule need to agree on the same target address;

  • higher-priority interface rules can still override the auto-generated ones;

  • for anything complex, manual rule management will save you from weird conflicts and mystery blocks down the line.

CrowdSec (the OPNsense plugin)

CrowdSec is a behavior-based protection layer - it watches your logs and automatically blocks suspicious activity. Unlike a classic firewall, it doesn't work off static IP lists. It works off behavior patterns instead: brute-force attempts, scanning, weird anomalous requests, that sort of thing.

The CrowdSec plugin installs straight from the official repos and bundles three components at once:

  • Log Processor (log analysis, formerly the IDS)
  • LAPI (a local API for decision-making)
  • Remediation Component (traffic blocking, formerly the IPS)

Installing It

Go to:

System → Firmware → Plugins

Find and install:

os-crowdsec

This automatically pulls in:

  • crowdsec
  • crowdsec-firewall-bouncer
  • os-crowdsec

⚠️ Important: resist the urge to start or configure any of this by hand from the shell. Everything CrowdSec-related in OPNsense goes through the plugin's own UI.

Confirming It Actually Installed

Refresh the page and head to:

Services → CrowdSec → Overview

From here you can check:

  • whether the Log Processor is running
  • whether LAPI is active
  • whether the Remediation Component is working
  • whether collections and scenarios have been loaded

If everything checks out, the base install's done.

CrowdSec Settings

Next stop:

Services → CrowdSec → Settings

Three core components are on by default:

  • Log Processor
  • LAPI
  • Remediation Component

Only turn these off for testing, or if you're running something non-standard (LAPI hosted elsewhere, say).

What It Does Out of the Box

Since CrowdSec 1.6.3, private IPs (your LAN ranges) get automatically excluded from blocking.

So addresses like:

  • 192.168.x.x
  • 10.x.x.x
  • 172.16.x.x

won't get blocked even if they trigger an attack scenario.

If you actually want internal addresses to be blockable, remove the whitelist parser responsible for that:

Testing That Remediation (IPS) Actually Works

You can add a manual test rule to check blocking is really firing.

⚠️ Important: running this command might kill your own SSH session.

Run it and:

  • your own IP gets banned for 2 minutes
  • you won't be able to reconnect from it during that window

Grabbing Your External IP

If you're on SSH, this'll get you your own IP:

or:

Remote LAPI (Optional)

By default, CrowdSec's local API (LAPI) just runs directly on OPNsense. For more elaborate setups, though, you can host it on a separate box entirely.

Worth doing if:

  • your OPNsense hardware is underpowered
  • you've already got a central CrowdSec server
  • you want one single place to manage everything

⚠️ Important: with a remote LAPI, some bits of the OPNsense UI (the machine and bouncer lists, for instance) may not display correctly.

Setting One Up

Assuming you've already got a separate LAPI server reachable over the network:

1. Configure the LAPI Server

On the CrowdSec server, open up:

Change:

for example:

Also update:

in the format:

Restart CrowdSec.

2. Configure OPNsense's Side

In OPNsense:

  • turn off Enable LAPI
  • turn on Manual LAPI configuration
  • apply
3. Register OPNsense With LAPI

On OPNsense, run:

4. Confirm It on the LAPI Server

If needed, approve it:

5. Add a Bouncer

You'll get back an API key, something like:

6. Configure the Bouncer on OPNsense

Open:

Fill in:

  • api_key
  • api_url

Restart the CrowdSec service:

or from the GUI:

Services → CrowdSec → Settings → Apply

Firewall Rules for Blocking Outbound Connections

By default, CrowdSec in OPNsense only blocks incoming connections from known-bad IPs. It doesn't cover the reverse case - something inside your network reaching out to one of those addresses on its own.

Think:

  • a compromised host on the LAN;
  • a malicious script or container;
  • someone accidentally running something sketchy.

In any of these, the connection gets through unless you've separately blocked outbound traffic to those known-bad IPs.

Floating Rules are the tool for this - they let you apply a single rule across multiple interfaces at once (LAN/VLAN).

Creating the Floating Rule

Go to:

Firewall → Rules → Floating

Click Add (+) top-right.

Set it up like so:

Parameter Value
Action Block
Interface LAN (or the relevant VLANs/interfaces)
Direction In
Protocol Any
Destination crowdsec_blacklists
Log Enabled
Description Block access to CrowdSec blacklist
IPv4 and IPv6

Running IPv6? You'll need a second rule for that traffic specifically.

OPNsense won't always automatically apply one rule to both stacks, so it's cleaner to split them:

  • one rule for IPv4
  • one for IPv6
Apply It

Once both rules exist, hit:

Apply Changes

From here on, anything inside your network trying to reach an IP on the CrowdSec blacklist gets stopped at the firewall.

Why This Actually Matters

This closes a real gap in coverage:

  • CrowdSec handles incoming traffic (internet → LAN)
  • Floating rules handle outgoing traffic (LAN → internet)

Together they cut down not just external attacks, but the blast radius if something inside your network does get compromised.

Blocking Known-Bad IPs with FireHOL

Even with a solid firewall config, you'll still see a steady trickle of connection attempts in your OPNsense logs from bots, scanners, and other unwelcome guests. You can't eliminate that traffic entirely, but you can cut it down a lot using public lists of IPs already known for bad behavior.

FireHOL is one of the more popular sources for this kind of thing. The project pulls together data from a bunch of threat-intelligence feeds and publishes ready-made lists of IPs tied to botnets, malware, C&C servers, scanners, and other assorted threats.

In OPNsense, you can add these lists as URL aliases, and the system will keep them downloaded and ready to use for filtering.

Setting Up a FireHOL Alias

Go to Firewall → Aliases, click Add.

Fill it in:

Field Value
Name Firehol
Type URL (IPs)

In Content, drop in the block lists you want:

Save, then click Apply so OPNsense goes and fetches these lists.

Excluding Your Own Networks

FireHOL's lists only contain public IPs anyway, but it's still good hygiene to explicitly exclude your internal ranges from the check.

Warning

Which FireHOL level should you choose? FireHOL aggregates dozens of different threat-intelligence sources and provides several blocking levels.

  • firehol_level1 - the most conservative list. It only includes IP addresses with a high threat reputation, so the risk of false positives is minimal. This is the level most users should go with.
  • firehol_level2 - includes more addresses and provides more aggressive filtering, but the chance of blocking legitimate resources goes up.
  • firehol_level3 - the strictest level. It combines a large number of sources and can trigger false positives, so it should only be used if you understand the potential consequences.
  • firehol_abusers_1d - a list of IP addresses seen engaging in suspicious activity over the last 24 hours. It's updated continuously and helps quickly block new attack sources.
  • For a home network or small infrastructure, firehol_level1 is usually enough. If you regularly see a lot of scans or password brute-force attempts, you can additionally add firehol_abusers_1d.
  • Level2 and level3 are best enabled only after evaluating the possible consequences and monitoring the firewall logs.

Create an alias for that:

Field Value
Name External
Type Networks

For the content, specify:

Then one more alias:

Field Value
Name Firehol_without_internal
Type Network Group

Add both External and Firehol to it.

The Actual Block Rule

Last step: the firewall rule itself.

Go to Firewall → Rules → WAN and add:

Field Value
Action Block
Interface WAN
Direction In
Protocol Any
Source Firehol_without_internal
Destination Any

Save, then Apply changes.

From now on, any incoming connection from an IP on FireHOL's lists gets blocked before anything else even gets evaluated.

Keeping the Lists Fresh

Attacker IPs churn constantly, so these lists need regular updates.

Go to System → Settings → Cron and set up a job:

Field Value
Enabled checked
Minutes 0
Hours 0
Day of the month *
Months *
Days of the week *
Command Update and reload firewall aliases

After this, OPNsense will grab the latest FireHOL lists every day and apply the updates on its own - no babysitting required.

Geoblock

Blocking by Country (GeoIP)

If your services are only meant for users in certain countries, geo-restriction is worth setting up. OPNsense does this via GeoIP aliases, which let firewall rules key off which country an IP belongs to.

Hooking Up the GeoIP Database

You'll need the MaxMind GeoLite2 database for this to work.

First, register on MaxMind's site and grab a personal license key. If you're in Russia, this can be a headache since MaxMind pulled registration for Russian users - but I'm sure you'll figure out a workaround.

Then go to Firewall → Aliases → GeoIP settings and in URL, paste a link like this, swapping in your own key for your-license-key:

Save.

Note

Since late 2023, MaxMind license keys expire every 90 days unless you confirm them by email. If your GeoIP auto-updates mysteriously stop working a few months from now, check your key's expiration first before you go digging through OPNsense's settings for a problem that isn't there.

More on that here.

Creating GeoIP Aliases

With the database hooked up, go to Firewall → Aliases and create:

Field Value
Name Geoblock
Type GeoIP (IPv4, IPv6)
Content Select the countries whose access you want to block

Want to explicitly allow one country instead? Create a second GeoIP alias. Say, for Russia:

Field Value
Name UK
Type GeoIP (IPv4, IPv6)
Content Russia

Building the Firewall Rules

Now for the matching firewall rules.

Go to Firewall → Rules → WAN and add a block rule:

Field Value
Action Block
Interface WAN
Direction In
TCP/IP Version IPv4 + IPv6
Protocol Any
Source Geoblock
Destination Any
Description Blocks specific countries

Need a specific service reachable only from one country? Add an allow rule:

Field Value
Action Pass
Interface WAN
Direction In
TCP/IP Version IPv4 + IPv6
Protocol TCP
Source RU
Destination WAN address
Destination port 443
Description Whitelist RU on port 443

Important. OPNsense evaluates rules top to bottom, so Pass needs to sit above Block - otherwise the connection gets killed before it ever reaches your allow rule.

Keeping the GeoIP Database Updated

MaxMind's database updates regularly, so set this up to refresh automatically.

Go to System → Settings → Cron and add a job:

Field Value
Enabled ✓
Minutes 0
Hours 0
Day of month *
Months *
Day of week *
Command Update and reload firewall aliases

From here, OPNsense pulls the latest GeoIP database daily and refreshes every alias built on geographic filtering.

Ad Blocking

Blocking Ads and Malicious Domains

One nice thing built into Unbound: support for DNS Block Lists (DNSBL). This lets you kill ads, trackers, malicious domains, and phishing sites right at the DNS resolution step, before clients even get a chance to connect.

First, make sure Unbound DNS is actually running.

Go to:

Services → Unbound DNS → General

and check Enable Unbound.

Go to:

Services → Unbound DNS → Blocklist

Turn on DNSBL and pick your block lists.
Parameter Value
Enable ✓
Type of DNSBL Toggle preferred lists

A good starting set:

  • Abuse.ch
  • OISD
  • AdAway
  • AdGuard
  • Blocklist.site

If turning this on breaks some site or service, add the offending domain to Whitelist Domains.

You can layer on more lists later, but I wouldn't flip on everything at once from the start - makes tracking down false positives a lot more annoying than it needs to be.

Keeping the Block Lists Fresh

Set these to update daily so they don't go stale.

Go to:

System → Settings → Cron

Set up a job:
Parameter Value
Minutes 0
Hours 0
Day of Month *
Months *
Day of Week *
Command Update Unbound DNSBLs
Description Update Unbound BLs

From here your DNS block lists will refresh automatically every day at 00:00.

NetFlow and Insight

NetFlow in OPNsense collects data about your network traffic - which devices and services are hogging bandwidth, when usage peaks, and exactly how traffic is being routed around.

The Insight module builds on top of that with graphs, reports, per-interface stats, and CSV export if you want to dig deeper in a spreadsheet or elsewhere.

Setting Up NetFlow

Go to Reporting → NetFlow and set:

Core Fields

Parameter Value
Listening interfaces LAN, WAN, and any other interfaces you want
WAN interfaces WAN
Capture local Enabled
Version v9
Destinations 127.0.0.1:2056

Apply this, and OPNsense starts collecting stats across every interface you listed and shipping the data to the local collector.

Checking It Out in Insight

Once NetFlow's running, the data shows up in the analytics module.

Go to:

Reporting → Insight

From here you can:

  • view network load graphs;

  • analyze traffic distribution across interfaces;

  • track load peaks;

  • export data as CSV for further digging.

Insight basically turns OPNsense into a lightweight network analytics tool - not just "what broke," but "what's actually running on this network, and how much of it."

Reporting Settings

OPNsense tracks system and interface stats through its built-in graphing engine (RRD - Round-Robin Database), which stores historical load data and renders it as graphs right in the web UI.

Unbound DNS Reporting

Running Unbound as your resolver? You can turn on stats collection for DNS queries.

Parameter Value
Statistics Enabled

Turn it on and OPNsense starts logging DNS query activity across the local network - handy for seeing which domains get hit most and how clients are actually behaving.

Reporting Database (RRD)

This next bit handles storing and rendering system performance graphs.

Parameter Value
Round-Robin-Database Enabled

RRD graphs your CPU load, memory usage, interfaces, and other system metrics. Data gets stored compactly and rolls over automatically as the database fills up.

Give it about a minute after changing graph settings before the new data shows up properly.

Split DNS

Split DNS in a Nutshell

The idea: the same domain (say, stilicho.ru) resolves to different answers depending on whether the client asking is on your internal network (LAN) or out on the internet.

Split DNS gives internal and external users different answers to the same query, so local requests to your own server never need to detour through the router. A few reasons this is worth doing:

  • Faster, since the router's no longer in the path.
  • A reverse proxy can cleanly tell internal and external requests apart and allow/deny accordingly, since NAT isn't in the mix.
  • Everything keeps working even with no internet access.
  • Still works even if your upstream DNS (ISP, Google, OpenDNS, whatever) goes down.

What You'll Need

  • An internal reverse proxy listening on port 80/443.
  • An internal DNS resolver that can do overrides, or host full DNS zones.

A Typical DNS Setup

For this example, domain.com is your domain, and 10.10.10.10 is your reverse proxy.

Go to Services > Unbound DNS > Overrides > Host Overrides > Add:

  • Host: *
  • Domain: stilicho.ru
  • Type: A or AAAA
  • IP: 10.10.10.10

Wrapping Up

That covers the "basic" OPNsense setup (and I use that word loosely at this point) - you should now have a working firewall with proper network segmentation and better-than-average security.

From here it's entirely up to your infrastructure and how far you want to push things - IDS/IPS is a natural next step, and honestly one you should add.

Worth remembering: OPNsense isn't some consumer plug-and-play router - it's a tool that reveals what it can do gradually, the deeper you get into it. The more you integrate it into your network, the more control you end up with over your own traffic and security.

item.title: History of OPNsense - From m0n0wall to a Modern Firewall
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: The history of the creation and development of OPNsense - a branch of the pfSense project that became an independent and actively developed open-source solution. We look at the reasons for the fork, the philosophy of the project, key stages of development, and how OPNsense differs from other open-source routers.
item.content:encoded:
History of OPNsense

Origins and motivation

The roots of OPNsense trace back to the m0n0wall project - a lightweight FreeBSD-based distribution designed for embedded systems and network gateways. It emerged back in the early 2000s and for years became the standard for anyone who needed a firewall running on decommissioned hardware without licensing headaches. Later, pfSense emerged from m0n0wall, which took over most of the audience and became, for a long time, the most popular platform for FreeBSD-based firewalls and routers. It was pfSense that many homelab enthusiasts encountered as "the only option" for a router OS as far back as ten years ago.

By the mid-2010s, part of the community and the developers behind pfSense began to diverge in their views on what the project's future should look like. It wasn't about one particular complaint, but a whole set of issues at once:

  • a more open development model, rather than decisions made behind closed doors by a single company;
  • a transparent licensing scheme without the risk that some functionality would suddenly move behind a paywall;
  • modern, secure code - at the time, pfSense's codebase seemed outdated to many;
  • a clear and predictable release structure.

In 2014, the Dutch company Deciso B.V. announced the creation of a new project - OPNsense, a fork of pfSense on FreeBSD, licensed under the BSD 2-Clause License, which allows free use, modification, and sale of the code, including commercial use, as long as attribution is retained (which is what OnlyOffice should have chosen from the start).

Project launch

  • Founding date: January 2, 2015
  • First release: OPNsense 15.1 Ascending Albatross (January 5, 2015)
  • Main project goals:
    • Security and code quality
    • Regular updates
    • An active community
    • A modern and clear web interface

Stages of development

The project grew quickly, establishing a clear release cycle:

  • two major releases per year - in January and July;
  • security updates every two weeks.

Key development milestones include moving to new FreeBSD versions, adopting HardenedBSD, an interface and API overhaul, and security improvements.

OPNsense release timeline

Version Codename Date Key highlights
15.1 Ascending Albatross Jan 2015 The project's first release
15.7 Brave Badger Jul 2015 Transition to a mature version
16.1 Crafty Coyote Jan 2016 Stability improvements
16.7 Dancing Dolphin Jul 2016 New networking features, UEFI support
17.1 Eclectic Eagle Jan 2017 Plugin support, PHP updates
17.7 Free Fox Jul 2017 Move to HardenedBSD, enhanced security
18.1 Groovy Gecko Jan 2018 Hardening of the kernel and security architecture
19.1 Inspiring Iguana Jan 2019 Alias API, HardenedBSD 11.2
19.7 Jazzy Jaguar Jul 2019 Updated interface, expanded logging
20.1 Keen Kingfisher Jan 2020 Last version with i386 support, improved GUI
20.7 Legendary Lion Jul 2020 HardenedBSD 12.1, Suricata 5, amd64-only
21.1 Marvelous Meerkat Jan 2021 UI improvements, updated firewall rules
21.7 Noble Nightingale Jul 2021 ZFS support, PHP 7.4 → Python 3.8
22.1 Observant Owl Jan 2022 Move to FreeBSD 13, IPv6 alias, RFC 5424 logging
22.7 Powerful Panther Jul 2022 FreeBSD 13.1, PHP 8.0, basic DDoS features
23.1 Quintessential Quail Jan 2023 PHP 8.1, WireGuard improvements, new API
23.7 Restless Roadrunner Jul 2023 OpenVPN improvements, PHP 8.2
24.1 Savvy Shark Jan 2024 Interface and performance improvements
24.7 Thriving Tiger Jul 2024 FreeBSD 14.1, Python 3.11, new Dashboard
25.1 Ultimate Unicorn Jan 2025 10th anniversary, FreeBSD 14.2, PHP 8.3, ZFS snapshot
25.7 Visionary Viper Jul 2025 FreeBSD 14.3, improved GUI, Alias acceleration
26.1 Witty Woodpecker Jan 2026 Dnsmasq as the default for DHCP, ISC DHCP - plugin only, Suricata 8, Firewall Rules redesign
26.7 Xenial Xenops Jul 2026 FreeBSD 15.1, OpenVPN 2.7, PHP 8.5, Python 3.13, Outbound NAT migration to Source NAT

Legal and organizational aspects

  • In 2017, Netgate (the creators of pfSense) lost a dispute over the opnsense.com domain.
    • WIPO (case D2017-1828) ruled that the domain should be transferred to Deciso.
    • This cemented the legal independence of the OPNsense brand.

The fact is, the legal dispute mentioned above was preceded by a rather unflattering episode. Netgate had managed to register the opnsense.com domain even before the project officially launched, and used it not as a neutral placeholder, but to publish critical material about the new fork - which many in the community saw not so much as an attempt to protect their own reputation, but as an attempt to slow down a competitor right out of the gate. The community did not look kindly on this behavior, and WIPO ultimately sided with OPNsense.

Project characteristics

Over more than ten years, OPNsense has developed a set of traits that set it apart not only from pfSense, but from most open-source router distributions in general.

Security is baked into the process here: security updates come out every two weeks rather than "whenever we absolutely have to," and the system's kernel has for years run on HardenedBSD - a fork of FreeBSD with additional memory protection mechanisms and address-space randomization. Modularity is implemented through a plugin system and an open API - you can bolt on functionality (WireGuard, IDS/IPS, proxy, 2FA) without having to patch the system by hand. Openness shows not only in the license, but in the fact that the project's roadmap is public, and community proposals actually make it into releases rather than sitting in some backlog. And finally, the BSD-2-Clause license - Deciso does have a paid Business Edition, but it's not a "crippled free version" with locked-away features, as is often the case with competitors: the difference is only a more conservative update pace and access to some commercial plugins (for example, Zenarmor, though it's also available in the free version) and support. The entire core firewall functionality is equally available in the community version.

Current state (2026)

  • Based on FreeBSD 15.1
  • Actively maintained by Deciso B.V.
  • A community of thousands of participants worldwide
  • Has a large number of ready-made plugins and integrations (WireGuard, Zenarmor, CrowdSec, and others)

Significance for the community

Over more than ten years, OPNsense has stopped being just "a pfSense fork for people annoyed at Netgate" and has become an independent project with its own audience, its own release cadence, and its own development philosophy. What started as an alternative is, for many, today a conscious first choice rather than a fallback option. What's more, a bit over two years ago, a mass exodus from PfSense began after they changed their software distribution terms.

Personally, what I find most interesting in this story isn't the domain dispute itself (the behavior of Netgate's head has long been a byword), but the fact that over the years the project has genuinely kept its pace: a release every six months, security patches every two weeks, and no drift toward "let's simplify things and put the complex stuff behind a paywall." That's exactly why, in my own Proxmox homelab, I ultimately settled on OPNsense as my main gateway - not because pfSense is bad in some way, but because I can see where each of these projects is heading, and I like the direction OPNsense is going.

If this history lesson has you wanting to actually try OPNsense, the best place to start is my OPNsense 26.1 install guide - it covers everything from a bare-metal install through firewall rules and attack protection.

Useful links

  • Official website
  • Documentation
  • Plugin list
  • Deciso B.V.
  • Historical article on PRWeb - 10 years of OPNsense
